transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-02-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Noah Kim (Redwood Solutions), Elaine Park (CTO, Nexa), Ravi Menon (Platform Eng, Nexa), Sammy Ortiz (ML Eng, Nexa)

--- Auto Summary (may be rough) ---
We talked about Nexa's bursty traffic for clinical-qa and chart-summarization services; main ask was how to avoid cold-KV penalties and prevent tail-latency spikes while keeping monthly cost under their 3% infra budget increase. Redwood proposed a 3 variant burst policy (conservative, balanced, aggressive) and a 72-hour reserved GPU trial for staging to run real traffic.

00:00 Maya: ok hey everyone thanks for jumping on i see we have the usual suspects, quick intros?
00:07 Elaine: hi this is elaine park, cto at nexa focusing on platform and privacy stuff
00:10 Ravi: ravi here, platform eng, i'll be leading the integration with our VPC
00:13 Sammy: sammy, ml engineer on the models and latency targets
00:16 Maya: and jordan li and noah from redwood se and solutions here to dig in, cool
00:21 Jordan: quick agenda — headroom forecasting, eviction policy options, k-v cache warmup, batching and quantization tradeoffs, q&a and next steps

02:05 Elaine: to set context we run two main endpoints: 1) chart-summarize that does long-context (avg 1.5k tokens) and 2) clinical-qa short queries (avg 120 tokens) both have diurnal spikes and occasional batch uploads from partner EHRs.
02:23 Ravi: spikes happen when billing jobs or report exports kick off, we sometimes see 5-10x baseline for 10-30 minutes. goal is to keep p99 under 800ms for clinical-qa and p95 under 3s for chart-summarize.

05:01 Jordan: alright so first principle — headroom = reserved capacity + prewarmed pools + acceptable queue depth. we model arrival as a nonstationary poisson with heavy tails, we built a simulator that can take your p95 arrival rate and burst multiplier to produce tail latency curves.
05:20 Sammy: can you explain the kv cache warmup assumption? our model uses a 2M token context across sessions so kv misses are a real pain
05:32 Jordan: yep, good q. our runtime treats KV cache at the sequence-block level; when a new request lands on a cold device we have to stream prefix blocks which adds a step function ~150-400ms depending on model size and network to K V store. in practice you recover after a few requests as KV is sticky to the pool. we simulate cold fraction decaying exponentially with a half-life parameter you can tune.
05:58 Maya: note i might say K V cache sometimes as K-V or kv, transcripts mess up the hyphen

08:40 Ravi: what about eviction? our worry is prewarming everything is cost prohibitive, but evicting too aggressively leads to repeated misses during a spike.
08:51 Jordan: evicting by LRU with size-based constraints is common; our additional knob is 'grace' — a short soft-sticky TTL where recently evicted slots can be rehydrated faster using a lightweight delta restore. practically that halves the cold miss penalty for bursts shorter than the grace window.
09:12 Elaine: is the grace window configurable per-pool? we have some pools dedicated to critical endpoints and others less so.
09:18 Jordan: yes per-pool. you can set aggressive eviction on low-priority pools and long grace on critical ones. also you can pin some models to reserved GPUs so their KV never goes cold.

12:00 Sammy: curious about quantization — we saw quality drift on our summarization when switching to int8. is Redwood recommending mixed-precision?
12:12 Jordan: short answer: for long-context summarization int8 sometimes hurts coherence. we recommend per-workload quant tunes — int8 for short-chat/qa, q4/x4 or 4-bit for long seq after evals. Redwood Optimize can run a sweep and produce a quality vs token-cost curve.

15:45 Ravi: can we see an example simulation for our traffic? like conservative vs balanced burst policy outcomes.
15:52 Noah: we have a workbook — link: https://redwood.example.com/simulations/nexa-workbook (shareable link). i'll attach after. the conservative policy keeps a warm prewarmed pool sized at 3x baseline concurrent requests with tight eviction; balanced uses demand-based autoscale with a 60s cooldown and grace window of 2 mins; aggressive allows prewarmed bursts plus ephemeral preemptible nodes.

19:10 Elaine: i want to be clear on failure modes — what happens when region goes down or we hit resource caps?
19:20 Jordan: two-layer fallback: vertical fallback to a smaller quantized variant (slightly higher latency but lower mem), and routing fallback to another region or dedicated cold queue. Redwood's routing policy can direct requests to a 'degraded' tier that caps tokens and applies stricter truncation to keep latency bounded.

22:30 Sammy: how do we avoid double-charging or inconsistent tokens when using reserved + burst ephemeral? i.e. billing complexity for us.
22:42 Maya: billing is usage based plus reserved capacity commitments. bursts on ephemeral preemptible are metered differently; we'll provide a sample cost model. for the trial we'll set up transparent billing so you can reconcile.

25:00 Ravi: security-wise our CISO will want KMS, SAML SSO and audit logs — on private deployment we need customer-managed KMS, is that possible?
25:11 Maya: yes private offers KMS/HSM integration and full audit logs retention, we'll send SOC2 docs and onboarding checklist. for hosted we support envelope encryption with customer KMS via our keywrap flow.

28:40 Jordan: back to headroom math — simple heuristic: size prewarmed = baseline_concurrency * peak_multiplier * model_latency_factor. ex: baseline 50 conc * 4x peak * 0.8 latency factor = 160 prewarmed slots. then tune with cooldowns and grace to trade cost vs p99. we typically run a 7-day replay in staging to pick the knob set.

31:12 Sammy: replay is good; can we run with sampled traffic instead of full PHI? we need to keep patient data private.
31:20 Maya: absolutely — use synthetic traffic or tokenized repros, we also support a local on-prem trial where replay runs inside your VPC, logs don't leave.

34:00 Ravi: question about queueing — do you see queue depth-based throttles helpful or is concurrency-limited pools better?
34:10 Jordan: both. concurrency-limited pools with a small soft queue gives predictable latency; pure token-throttles are more complex. Redwood's scheduler exposes per-route queue depth, request priority and fairness. for latency SLOs we prefer concurrency caps + backpressure.

37:50 Elaine: during spikes with partner uploads, arrival is bursty but predictable. can we pre-warm using signals?
37:59 Jordan: yes event-driven prewarm — webhook from your ingestion pipeline can call Redwood's prewarm API to provision ephemeral prewarmed slots. that avoids constant warm pools and is cost efficient if spikes are infrequent.

41:20 Sammy: about KV cache placement — does Redwood store KV in local GPU memory or external store? implications for warmup time?
41:28 Jordan: KV is stored in accelerator memory for fastest reads; the prefix transfer is over internal network when moving between hosts. the warmup time depends on model shard size; large LLMs with multi-GPU sharding have longer prefix restore times. our simulation uses measured restore latencies by model family.

45:00 Ravi: can you show impact of quantization on memory footprint and consequent pool sizing?
45:10 Jordan: for example, moving from fp16 to int8 reduces model footprint ~2x-3x depending on architecture; that increases possible prewarmed slots per GPU, reducing reserved capacity costs. but remember inference compute changes and kernel selection can alter latency; sometimes quantization yields small p95 regressions. we'll include sample numbers in the workbook.

48:30 Elaine: what's the recommended guardrail for grace windows? too long and we keep cold memory hogs, too short and we see repeat misses.
48:40 Jordan: start with grace = median burst length * 1.5. if bursts are 10-30 minutes set grace to 20 minutes for critical pools, lower for low priority. then iterate with simulations.

52:00 Noah: quick demo — (screen share described) workbook showing baseline 200 req/min, 6x burst for 15 minutes, p99 moves from 620ms to 1.8s under conservative but 720ms under balanced with 2-min grace (numbers approximated).

58:10 Sammy: these numbers look good but what about degradation under quantization?
58:20 Jordan: in that workbook the int8 variant adds ~120ms p99 for chart-summarize, but halves cost per token. tradeoff is workload dependent — we'll run your eval set and post evaluation reports.

61:44 Ravi: operations question — how quickly can we change eviction policies in prod if we see issues?
61:52 Jordan: policy changes are config-only and roll out in seconds; actual pool behavior converges in minutes. we also provide safe-rollback to previous policy.

65:10 Elaine: ok wrap, i want a clear proposal for conservative/balanced/aggressive with estimated monthly cost deltas and SLO hit probabilities. can you get that to us?
65:20 Maya: yes we'll produce the three variants, cost and SLO impact, plus a recommended initial setup for staging (72-hour reserved + prewarm webhook)
65:38 Elaine: also need SOC2 and KMS docs and a contact for legal procurement
65:42 Maya: we'll attach docs and loop in our security lead, and i will be primary procurement contact.
